teaser:open.text: Hypercomb. A new way to be.

teaser:hive.text: Your work lives on a grid of hexagons, on your own machine. Click a tile and you travel into it.

teaser:presence.text: There is no server and no account. It runs in your browser, and nothing leaves until you say so.

teaser:signature.text: Everything has one kind of name: a signature, computed from the content itself. Same content, same name, on every machine. You verify instead of trusting.

teaser:open-source.text: It is open source, and every feature is a signed module — so a fork is something you can prove.

teaser:close.text: Type a name, press Enter, and you have a hive. Hypercomb — the hive is yours.

scene:02.text: Hypercomb is not an app you sign up for. It is an open protocol: a shared way to name, keep and pass on what people make, that anyone can use and no one owns. Three ideas carry it. Every piece of work is named by a fingerprint of its own content. Every change is kept. And work travels between people directly, from device to device and domain to domain. The code is public, under a licence that keeps every copy open.
scene:02.take: the take jwize chose on 2026-11-26 (voice/voxtral/local2), re-cut at its word edges

scene:12.text: Your hive is your workbench, and it is files on your own device. It keeps working if any company disappears, because no company sits in the middle. You can export it, inspect it and move it. Nothing leaves until you publish it.

scene:03.text: Here is what it looks like. Your work sits on a grid of tiles. A tile can hold anything: a note, a picture, a document, a game, a whole website. Open a tile and you step inside it, and every tile can hold a grid of its own. Tiles inside tiles, as deep as you need. What you see was recorded live.

scene:04.text: There is no account and no sign-up. Hypercomb runs in your browser, with a desktop app on the way, and your work is kept on your device. When you share, your work goes to a host: your own machine, your own domain, or the host of a friend you trust. Presence is permission: your work is where you are, and it leaves only when you share it. It is free and open source, written in plain words so anyone can follow it.

scene:05.text: Every piece of content gets its address from the content itself: a signature, computed from its bytes. The same content always gets the same signature, on any machine. Change one byte and the signature changes. So a signature proves what it names: you never have to trust where a file came from, because your own device can check it. And a file used a hundred times is stored once. In technical terms, the signature is the SHA-256 hash of the bytes.

scene:06.text: Underneath it all is one pattern. A tile has a name. What it holds is named by a fingerprint of its content. And what it holds can be more tiles, built the same way. That is all of it. A note, a website, a whole community: each is this one pattern, repeated. In technical terms, it is a content-addressed tree, where names point to signatures and every node has the same shape.

scene:07.text: Every change you make becomes a new layer: a complete record of that place at that moment. Nothing is overwritten. The history of a place is a numbered list, and the newest entry is how it looks now. Undo is simply reading an earlier step. You can rewind a page, restore any moment, or save a snapshot before you try something bold. It works like version control, for everything you make, not only for code.

scene:08.text: Hypercomb uses a few exact words, and each means one thing. A hive is your own place, kept on your device. A tile is one piece of content. A layer is one moment of a place, kept for good. A signature is the name content gives itself. A bee is a small piece of behaviour that acts when it is needed, or when you say its word. A pheromone is a signed mark of interest left on content, so people with matching interests can find it; carrying it to them is still being built. Replication is how work moves between hives, checked byte by byte. The brood is where code from someone else waits, and never runs, until you accept it. And a colony is a domain with the hives it hosts; there are many, and none of them is in charge.

scene:09.text: Behavior in Hypercomb lives in bees, short for beehavior: small, self-contained parts that act when they are needed, or when you say their word. Navigation, editing, games, the words you type: all of them are bees, and what still sits in the shell is moving out into bees too. Each one is named by its signature, so anyone can read it, improve it, and share it back. And a bee from a stranger does not just run. Before you take it, you can try it on their domain, and have your own A.I. read it for you. Once you take it, it waits, held, until your own hand accepts it.

scene:10.text: Making something takes one gesture: type a name and press Enter. That is a tile. Type three more names and you have a structure. Reading works the same way for everyone, person or program: take a name, find its newest layer, and read what it holds. One act, used for everything. Even this presentation lives in a hive, as tiles.

scene:11.text: You can do almost everything by saying it. The command line reads plain words: type a name to make a tile, or a slash and a word to act. Say website, and a hive's pages show as a site. Because every act is a sentence, you can see what it will touch before it runs, repeat it, and teach it to someone else. The sentence is the program. Communities translate the words into their own languages.

scene:13.text: Everything has its place by its name, and every byte can be checked, so nothing has to be taken on trust. When someone shares work with you, you receive signatures, and your device checks each piece as it arrives. Content used in many places is stored once, and any host that holds it can hand you a copy. A copy from any host is as good as the original, because it proves itself.

scene:14.text: Reason three: time is on your side. Undo works across sessions. A rewind window lets you scrub through what a page used to look like. When you take someone's work, it arrives as a named revision, and any update they make later waits until you choose it. Snapshots let you try something risky, then come back. Every step is kept unless you choose to destroy it, so the past is one signature away, and it never rots.

scene:15.text: Your domain is your front door. Hypercomb takes you there in steps: start in your browser, share through a friend's host, then run your own host under your own domain. The people who follow your domain get your work straight from you, and your community can connect to the communities it cares about most, domain to domain. No platform stands between you and the people you choose.

scene:16.text: And here is the first thing anyone sees. Remember the simplest pattern: a name, and what it holds, named by its own signature. Read from outside, every hive is exactly that: an index of names and signatures. That index is called a Hyperdex, from hyper and index. It is not something built beside your hive. It is your hive, seen from the door. The root of your domain serves it, signed, and it is the first impression anyone has of you. What it shows depends on who is looking: a stranger sees your showcase, and you see your whole network, one domain to a row. And it can take many shapes, a list, a honeycomb, a wall of cards, with your business card as one entry among them. Visit someone's domain, and their Hyperdex is how they greet you.

scene:17.text: Shared work is carried by the people who use it. Hosts are run by those people, and publishing puts each piece up under its own signature before a pointer moves to the new version, so older versions keep working. Work is copied from host to host, and every copy is checked against its signature, so the more people care about something, the more places it lives. Trust is an allowance you give each peer, never a switch that is on by default. And nothing about you is tracked: not one statistic is collected. Your work is served by everyone who cares about it, and kept safe by your peers.

scene:18.text: Working together happens directly between people. Open a swarm, and everyone in the room sees each other's tiles live. Take what you want, and it lands in your own hive. When someone leaves, their tiles leave with them. When work should stay, you publish it to a host. Either way, it moves from hive to hive by its signature and is checked when it arrives. No feed decides what you see.

scene:19.text: A.I. agents now act for people almost everywhere. In Hypercomb, an agent speaks the same sentences you do, under the same rules. You choose the model: one in the cloud with your own key, or one that runs on your own machine. It reads only what you allow, and proposes what to change. Inside your hive, history can undo anything it does, and anything that would leave your device waits for you to accept it.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive#1.text: One tile in its editor: a name, a picture, a border, a link, and its words. Every tile is these same few parts.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/word#1.text: You name a tile by typing a word, written however you like.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/word#2.text: The hive folds it first: lower case, one hyphen between words, and stray marks dropped.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/word#3.text: Then the folded word is signed, and that signature is the word's address.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/word#4.text: Ann and Bo type it their own way, in hives of their own, and each folds it the same.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/word#5.text: Each signs it alone, and all three land on one address, with no registry to ask.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/layer#1.text: A tile and the tiles under it are written down as one small document: its layer.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/layer#2.text: It holds the tile's name, then each child by a signature, never the child itself.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/layer#3.text: Name first, then every field in the same order, so the same layer always gets the same signature.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/layer#4.text: However much its children hold, a layer stays small, and it reads complete on its own.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/layer#5.text: To go deeper, you follow one signature to the next small document, and only when you need it.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/layer#6.text: Humanity centres and the words under it, from a hive in use. Each of them can hold a layer of its own.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/meta#1.text: In a layer, a reference names not the picture itself, but a small envelope around it: the meta.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/meta#2.text: The envelope says what kind of thing it points at: a layer, bytes, a dependency, or a behaviour.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/meta#3.text: Exactly one of the four is filled in, and its signature is the one place to go next.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/meta#4.text: It also says how the layer holds the picture: here, as its background.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/meta#5.text: The picture itself is never touched: meaning is wrapped around the content, never written inside it.

beat:protocol/simple/primitive/meta#6.text: A child is held the same way: an envelope around a layer, which holds envelopes of its own.

beat:protocol/simple/opening#1.text: The opening builds a cube before anything else, and it starts from one hexagon and its word.

beat:protocol/simple/opening#2.text: Its layer gives the first direction: a row of words, then rows under rows.

beat:protocol/simple/opening#3.text: Its signature gives the second: each word's versions, climbing into a column.

beat:protocol/simple/opening#4.text: Origin, where a tile came from, gives the third: the same word, held in more than one hive.

beat:protocol/simple/opening#5.text: Move six adds no part at all, and move seven turns whatever a meta says into one more direction.

beat:protocol/simple/opening#6.text: So every tile you open after this is one point of a cube you have watched being built.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/hexagon#1.text: It begins with one hexagon, and the word on it is hypercomb.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/hexagon#2.text: Open it, and it shows four parts: its word, its signature, its meta, and its layer.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/hexagon#3.text: Its layer is empty, and so is its meta: nothing sits under it, and nothing says what it means.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/hexagon#4.text: So its signature is worked out from the word alone.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/hexagon#5.text: No other kind of thing will appear: every move after this is these four parts again.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/hexagon#6.text: This is hypercomb, and for now it is only a name.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/row#1.text: Now hypercomb's layer fills, and the words under it lay out side by side.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/row#2.text: Read across, they make a sentence: hypercomb is simple, organized, collaborative, intelligent, accessible and localized.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/row#3.text: Each one is a tile just like hypercomb, with a word, a signature, a meta and a layer of its own.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/row#4.text: Across the row is the first direction: words beside words, under the same word.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/row#5.text: A layer is the words that sit under one word.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/stack#1.text: Tilt the row, and it becomes a plane: hypercomb's layer, seen from the side.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/stack#2.text: Every word on it is a tile, so every word opens onto a row of its own.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/stack#3.text: Some of those words hold rows as well, and the single plane becomes a stack of planes.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/stack#4.text: Follow one path down and it reads as a phrase: hypercomb is simple, shown by the primitive, made of a word.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/stack#5.text: Going deeper adds nothing new: each level is a word holding a layer, exactly like the first.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/stack#6.text: Every word can hold a layer of its own.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/column#1.text: Change something in simple, and its layer is written again, with a new signature.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/column#2.text: The old layer is not touched. It stays where it was, and the new one sits on top.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/column#3.text: Every word changes the same way, so each one grows a column as tall as its own history.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/column#4.text: The top of each column is its heart: what every read lands on, and what a publish points to.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/column#5.text: The columns line up only for your eye. One word's second step has nothing to do with another's.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/column#6.text: Nothing is replaced. Every change is kept, one above the other.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/spread#1.text: Here is simple again: the column you made.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/spread#2.text: Someone you follow made a simple of their own, and it can stand beside yours.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/spread#3.text: Neither replaces the other. Each keeps its own history and its own heart, at the same word.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/spread#4.text: Where each one came from is a mark it wears, called its origin.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/spread#5.text: An origin can be a chain: bo's simple reached you through ann, and its thread runs back through both.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/spread#6.text: The same word can come from many hands.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/fill#1.text: Shrink each tile to a point: one word, at one version, from one hand.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/fill#2.text: The words still run across, and each word's versions still climb above it.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/fill#3.text: Behind simple, the other hands' columns stand where they stood.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/fill#4.text: Do the same for every word, and every hand behind it, and the points fill a cube.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/fill#5.text: Nobody drew that cube. It is the primitive, repeated in three directions.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/tesseract#1.text: Open one point, and its meta layer says more about it.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/tesseract#2.text: Locale, platform and audience are marks a point can wear, just as origin is, and each can divide the points.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/tesseract#3.text: Any three can be drawn as the cube's directions. Here they are word, version and origin.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/tesseract#4.text: Add a fourth, and a second cube appears inside the first, each point joined to its twin.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/tesseract#5.text: That is a tesseract. Every further mark is one more direction of the same shape.

beat:protocol/simple/opening/tesseract#6.text: Everything here is the same thing, used again.

beat:protocol/simple#1.text: Here is what it looks like. Your work sits on a grid of tiles. A tile can hold anything: a note, a picture, a document, a game, a whole website. Open a tile and you step inside it, and every tile can hold a grid of its own. These tiles come from a hive in use: a cigar journal, a library of knowledge, a room for hosting. Tiles inside tiles, as deep as you need.

beat:protocol/accessible#1.text: Accessible means this is for as many people as possible, and for everyone if we can manage it.

beat:protocol/accessible#2.text: Reading needs no account: a published presentation opens in any browser.

beat:protocol/accessible#3.text: Every page can be listened to, one plain sentence at a time, with the words shown as they are spoken.

beat:protocol/accessible#4.text: It fits a phone, one column at a time.

beat:protocol/accessible#5.text: The arrow keys step through a page, so it works without a mouse.

beat:protocol/accessible#6.text: If you ask your device for less motion, the pictures hold still and nothing is lost.

beat:protocol/accessible#7.text: And we keep simplifying: a page that is not clear gets changed.

beat:protocol/accessible#8.text: This is not finished. These pages have not yet been tested with a screen reader, and that work is ahead.

beat:protocol/accessible#9.text: Forty-five lessons, open beside the hive itself. Each one opens the real thing, and puts it away again.

beat:protocol/localized#1.text: Every word the hive itself shows you is looked up in your language, each time it is drawn.

beat:protocol/localized#2.text: Beneath lie the words the hive ships with, and where your language has a gap, English shows through.

beat:protocol/localized#3.text: The community fills those gaps, and only those, with words its translators publish.

beat:protocol/localized#4.text: Any word you set for yourself lies on top of everything else.

beat:protocol/localized#5.text: Read down each column, and the first word found is the one you see.

beat:protocol/localized#6.text: After language ja, the hive’s own reference speaks Japanese, here filtered to the words about tiles.

beat:protocol/simple/act#1.text: Hover a tile and its acts appear: shelf, edit, website, notes, link, remove. Each is also a word you can type.

beat:protocol/organized/history#1.text: One layer with 478 versions, newest on top. Each is a step you can go back to, and none is ever removed.

beat:protocol/organized/build#1.text: One pass of work often changes many tiles at once: here, three of the opening's seven moves.

beat:protocol/organized/build#2.text: Say builds and a name, and the whole branch is sealed into one signature that covers every tile in it.

beat:protocol/organized/build#3.text: The name and that signature are kept on the branch itself, as one record in its list of builds.

beat:protocol/organized/build#4.text: Seal it again with nothing changed, and nothing is added, because the same tiles give the same signature.

beat:protocol/organized/build#5.text: Builds revert brings an older build back, after it first records where you are now.

beat:protocol/organized/build#6.text: It lands as the newest step, and the build you left stays in the list, ready to bring back.

beat:protocol/organized/layout#1.text: A layout is a short list of words, kept on a tile: the words its layer shows, in order.

beat:protocol/organized/layout#2.text: Say layout on, and only the children those words name are shown, seated in the list's order.

beat:protocol/organized/layout#3.text: The rest are left out, untouched: say layout off, and every child shows again.

beat:protocol/organized/layout#4.text: Every switch is a new version of the layer, so a layout undoes like any other change.

beat:protocol/organized/layout#5.text: The list has a signature of its own, so another tile can take the same layout, word for word.

beat:protocol/organized/layout#6.text: Layout on shows the six named words in order; layout off shows every child again. Nothing was deleted or moved.

beat:protocol/organized/trait#1.text: A trait is a word a tile leaves open, so you can see what it wants before anything fills it.

beat:protocol/organized/trait#2.text: A child with that name fills it: here, the card's own child called portrait.

beat:protocol/organized/trait#3.text: Or you choose a filler yourself, from anywhere in your hive, and your choice comes first.

beat:protocol/organized/trait#4.text: Hide contact's tile, and its place stays: a silhouette waits there, and pressing it makes the tile again.

beat:protocol/organized/trait#5.text: A trait is a mark, never a parent, so the portrait stands on its own and can fill another creation too.

beat:protocol/organized/trait#6.text: Three traits given, one tile hidden: contact stays as a silhouette, a place still open for whatever fills it.

beat:protocol/organized/organization#1.text: Here are four pieces, each kept where it was made, and each one standing on its own.

beat:protocol/organized/organization#2.text: A website is one way to organize them: it shows three of them, in an order of its own.

beat:protocol/organized/organization#3.text: Each piece wears a small mark for that website, holding its place, so the order lives on the mark.

beat:protocol/organized/organization#4.text: A question is another way: every piece that carries a word, gathered in one flat list.

beat:protocol/organized/organization#5.text: The photo and the map sit in both at once, and neither the website nor the question owns them.

beat:protocol/organized/organization#6.text: Make a new organization any time: the old one can stay beside it, and removing either removes no piece.

beat:protocol/organized/organization#7.text: The same tile opened as a website: a card made of its own pieces. Switch back, and the hexagons are all still there.

beat:protocol/collaborative/domain#1.text: Revolución, a cigar journal built as a hive for its own domain: the journal, the flavour wheel, the lounge and the store are all tiles.

beat:protocol/collaborative/trial#1.text: A change you want people to try opens at its own address: the word try, a dash, and the site's name.

beat:protocol/collaborative/trial#2.text: That address is its own origin, so nothing it does can reach anyone's hive.

beat:protocol/collaborative/trial#3.text: The host refuses every write from it, and it holds no keys to sign with.

beat:protocol/collaborative/trial#4.text: Meanwhile the live name keeps pointing at what people run today.

beat:protocol/collaborative/trial#5.text: Only you, the publisher, can promote it, and promoting moves the live name to the files the trial already ran.

beat:protocol/collaborative/trial#6.text: Nothing is rebuilt or sent again, so the site now runs exactly what was tried.

beat:protocol/collaborative/publishing#1.text: From a hive in use: its domains, how replication works, and the shared pieces it is built from, each one a tile.

beat:protocol/collaborative/participant#.text: Ann serves a creation from her own domain: one tile, and the pieces under it.
Bo takes it whole, every piece as she made it, so it runs for him exactly as it runs for her.
You have your own build of cards, and you take only the one piece of hers you want.
It lands at its own place in your build, and every other piece stays exactly as it was.
When you commit, your mix becomes a build of its own, with its own signature, ready to share.
So everyone mixes the pieces that suit them, and each mix still says which piece came from whom.

beat:protocol/collaborative/sharing#1.text: Look inside a card: it holds no colors of its own, only the words it needs, surface and primary.

beat:protocol/collaborative/sharing#2.text: A menu needs primary and outline, and neither part knows the other is there.

beat:protocol/collaborative/sharing#3.text: Those words belong to neither side, so anything that answers them will fit.

beat:protocol/collaborative/sharing#4.text: A theme is simply a set of answers, one for every word.

beat:protocol/collaborative/sharing#5.text: Choose another theme, and that one choice is all that changes, with no part opened or rewired.

beat:protocol/collaborative/sharing#6.text: Everything that names those words follows at once, dressed in the new answers.

beat:protocol/collaborative/hosting#1.text: Without a host, your hive sees only what the people online beside it are showing, for as long as they stay.

beat:protocol/collaborative/hosting#2.text: A host keeps pools of meaning: a word, answered at one address that every host derives the same way.

beat:protocol/collaborative/hosting#3.text: Ask any host for that address, and it lists what it holds there, from whoever made it.

beat:protocol/collaborative/hosting#4.text: Your hive asks every host it follows, and finds those pieces whether or not their makers are online.

beat:protocol/collaborative/hosting#5.text: Each piece is checked by its signature and each maker by their own signed index, so no host can make one up.

beat:protocol/collaborative/hosting#6.text: Running a host, or joining one, is what gives your hive that reach.

beat:protocol/collaborative/tapestry#1.text: Every hive has the same shape, and each one holds pieces of its own.

beat:protocol/collaborative/tapestry#2.text: Your hive and Ann's both hold this piece: the same bytes, so the same signature.

beat:protocol/collaborative/tapestry#3.text: That match is the thread, and nobody has to draw it, store it, or keep it up.

beat:protocol/collaborative/tapestry#4.text: Ann shares another piece with Bo, Bo shares one with Cy, and every match is one more thread.

beat:protocol/collaborative/tapestry#5.text: Followed outward from your hive, the threads weave one picture, larger than any hive, that nobody owns.

beat:protocol/collaborative/tapestry#6.text: And a new hive is woven in the moment it takes a single piece from anyone.

beat:protocol/localized/translating#1.text: A translator writes the words her language is missing, in her own hive, as her own.

beat:protocol/localized/translating#2.text: She says language offer, names a host, and her words travel there as one catalog, signed under her key.

beat:protocol/localized/translating#3.text: The host lists every catalog for that language, checking each translator's signature again before it lists one.

beat:protocol/localized/translating#4.text: You say language sync, and your hive reads the hosts you follow, keeping a catalog only if every byte matches its name.

beat:protocol/localized/translating#5.text: Say language missing and name a host, and it learns which words you still lack, so translators see where they are needed.

beat:protocol/localized/translating#6.text: Only a person can say these words, so nothing is sent or placed until someone chooses to.

beat:protocol/localized/locale#1.text: A tile has one name, and it keeps that name in every language.

beat:protocol/localized/locale#2.text: Lay the languages down the side, and each place a name meets a language holds one reading.

beat:protocol/localized/locale#3.text: Say language, then Japanese, and every tile is drawn again in its Japanese reading, in a single pass.

beat:protocol/localized/locale#4.text: A tile can carry its own words for a language, and they come before anyone else's.

beat:protocol/localized/locale#5.text: Where no reading exists, the tile simply shows its name, so nothing is ever left blank.

beat:protocol/localized/locale#6.text: Your language changes how the hive reads to you, never what anything is.

beat:protocol/intelligent/debugging#1.text: When something breaks, say module trials, and see every change people are already trying, and what each touches.

beat:protocol/intelligent/debugging#2.text: Say module changes and its name, and read that one change file by file: what went out, what came in.

beat:protocol/intelligent/debugging#3.text: Say module audit, and your own A.I. reads what it would bring beside what you run, and runs none of it.

beat:protocol/intelligent/debugging#4.text: Say module take, and that change comes into your own hive, held until you accept it.

beat:protocol/intelligent/debugging#5.text: If it was the wrong guess, say module drop, and after a reload, that place runs as it did before.

beat:protocol/intelligent/debugging#6.text: You try one change at a time, so when it works, you know exactly which change fixed it.

beat:protocol/intelligent/merging#1.text: You and someone else each changed the same file, starting from the same version.

beat:protocol/intelligent/merging#2.text: Today both stay whole, side by side, and since one place runs one version, only one can run there.

beat:protocol/intelligent/merging#3.text: Say module focus, and the hive already names two trials that change the same file as a clash.

beat:protocol/intelligent/merging#4.text: What is planned: the A.I. reads all three versions, and drafts one that keeps both changes.

beat:protocol/intelligent/merging#5.text: Like any draft, it would wait for you to accept it, or to keep your own.

beat:protocol/intelligent/merging#6.text: Either way, nothing is overwritten: every version, and the draft, keeps its own signature.

beat:protocol/accessible/reader#1.text: Open a published presentation, and your browser asks one host for it: the one whose address you opened.

beat:protocol/accessible/reader#2.text: Everything the page shows comes back from that host: its words, its typefaces, its voice and its pictures.

beat:protocol/accessible/reader#3.text: An ordinary page would also call out to a font service, a script library and a visitor counter.

beat:protocol/accessible/reader#4.text: Here, the door a reader comes in by refuses them: it fetches nothing from any host but its own.

beat:protocol/accessible/reader#5.text: And the presentation's own check fails any page that names another host for even one of its parts.

beat:protocol/accessible/reader#6.text: So reading tells no one but the host you chose to read.

beat:protocol/accessible/listening#1.text: Every page here is told in beats, and each beat is one plain sentence.

beat:protocol/accessible/listening#2.text: When a beat has been recorded, you hear it in the same voice that tells the tour.

beat:protocol/accessible/listening#3.text: You read it too: the caption says the same words, and a screen reader announces each one.

beat:protocol/accessible/listening#4.text: And the part of the picture it speaks of lights up while it is said.

beat:protocol/accessible/listening#5.text: Turn the voice off, and the words stay; each one waits as long as it takes to read.

beat:protocol/accessible/listening#6.text: So every sentence is written for the ear: no symbols, no tables, nothing a voice would stumble on.

beat:protocol/accessible/phone#1.text: On a wide screen, a second panel, like a picture from the hive, stands beside the figure.

beat:protocol/accessible/phone#2.text: Its words are sized from the page's own width, not the window's, so it fits alone or inside a hive.

beat:protocol/accessible/phone#3.text: When that width narrows to a phone, the panel moves under the figure, into one column.

beat:protocol/accessible/phone#4.text: There the caption is given more room, and the step counter gives way to the controls.

beat:protocol/accessible/phone#5.text: The presentation's own check opens every page at a phone's width, and fails any page that scrolls sideways.

beat:protocol/accessible/phone#6.text: So a phone gets the whole page, not a lesser one: the same words and pictures, one column at a time.

beat:protocol/accessible/motion#1.text: Some people feel unwell when things slide and fade, so their device can ask every page for less motion.

beat:protocol/accessible/motion#2.text: With motion, the lit part fades up, a line draws itself, and the caption rises into place.

beat:protocol/accessible/motion#3.text: With less motion, the same part is simply lit, the line is already whole, and the caption is just there.

beat:protocol/accessible/motion#4.text: Nothing is lost: the last picture is the same either way, and only the in-between is gone.

beat:protocol/accessible/motion#5.text: And a page that would play by itself waits instead, for you to step through at your own pace.

beat:protocol/accessible/motion#6.text: Every page in this presentation keeps this rule, and the narrated tour stops its sliding and fading too.

beat:protocol/intelligent/sentence#1.text: An agent asks to say three lines. They wait on the command line in plain words until a person presses Enter.

beat:protocol/intelligent/agent#1.text: A side session asked to add three meetups. Its lines were shown first, a person pressed Enter, and every line is kept.

beat:protocol/collaborative/gate#1.text: Three gates stand between someone else's work and your hive, and each one asks its own question.

beat:protocol/collaborative/gate#2.text: The first is whom you take from: your hive asks only the hosts and people you have chosen, and never everyone.

beat:protocol/collaborative/gate#3.text: The second is what you keep: what arrives is judged by the marks it wears, and until you name an interest, everything is kept.

beat:protocol/collaborative/gate#4.text: The third is what may run: once your hive is running, a package from another domain becomes your running code only when a publisher you follow has signed for it.

beat:protocol/collaborative/gate#5.text: A piece you pick by hand from anyone else is held, and it does not run until you accept it yourself.

beat:protocol/collaborative/gate#6.text: Keeping something never makes it run, and publishing it is a separate choice again.

beat:protocol/collaborative/gate#7.text: The first two gates are built, and the third is partly built: its rule holds when a package is installed, some other paths are still open, and a screen for your own rules is planned.

beat:protocol/organized/hiding#1.text: A list that lets you get rid of something offers one act, and that act is hide.

beat:protocol/organized/hiding#2.text: Hiding takes it out of the list and changes nothing else, so one press brings it back.

beat:protocol/organized/hiding#3.text: What you hid collects in a delete area, a fold you open on purpose.

beat:protocol/organized/hiding#4.text: Deleting exists only there, and the hive refuses to delete a thing that was not hidden first.

beat:protocol/organized/hiding#5.text: Delete means this hive forgets it: the same bytes held anywhere else stay valid, and can still be fetched by their signature.

beat:protocol/organized/hiding#6.text: Today a host's list of builds and a branch's published versions work this way, and any list added later must follow the same rule.

beat:protocol/organized/hiding#7.text: The rule binds the builders too: no update and no test may wipe your tiles, your history or your pools.

beat:protocol/organized/shelf#1.text: A tile is stored once, and a page only lists it, so the same tile can show in many places.

beat:protocol/organized/shelf#2.text: So nothing here is copied or cut: placing a tile adds one more place where it shows.

beat:protocol/organized/shelf#3.text: The shelf is a strip at the top of the screen that holds the tiles you are carrying.

beat:protocol/organized/shelf#4.text: Sending a tile to the shelf takes a reference and writes nothing, so the page it came from is untouched.

beat:protocol/organized/shelf#5.text: Only the drop writes: drop it to show the tile here as well, or hold Shift to move it here.

beat:protocol/organized/shelf#6.text: Recents shows every tile a hive ever made, once each, newest at the centre, with hidden ones shaded and never absent.

beat:protocol/organized/shelf#7.text: The shelf and recents are built, and choosing which look a tile lands with is not built yet.

beat:protocol/intelligent/interest#1.text: A pheromone is a small signed signal, left on a piece of content, that says this is worth attention.

beat:protocol/intelligent/interest#2.text: Anyone can leave one: you, another person, or an agent that read the content.

beat:protocol/intelligent/interest#3.text: It never says what a thing is: that is the name's job, so a new grouping gets a name, never a new kind of signal.

beat:protocol/intelligent/interest#4.text: Your interests are a private list of the signals you watch for and the ones you never want, and the list never leaves your hive.

beat:protocol/intelligent/interest#5.text: Only a match brings content forward for you, and where nothing matches, nothing is hidden from you.

beat:protocol/intelligent/interest#6.text: Signing, checking and reading these signals in your own hive is built, and until you name an interest, nothing is filtered.

beat:protocol/intelligent/interest#7.text: A signal is meant to travel with its content from one hive to another, and that part is planned, not built.

beat:protocol/simple/proof#1.text: A signature is worked out from the bytes alone, so anyone holding the bytes can work it out again and trust nobody.

beat:protocol/simple/proof#2.text: A list of what a folder holds is never proof: a host can list anything, and nothing in a listing is signed.

beat:protocol/simple/proof#3.text: A pool is where things of one meaning gather, and it holds membership, never truth: the truth stays in the layers.

beat:protocol/simple/proof#4.text: Membership becomes proof in two ways only: a mark inside the member's own bytes, or a signed list of the whole set.

beat:protocol/simple/proof#5.text: Not every pool has that form yet, and where it does not, the listing is only one host's memory.

beat:protocol/simple/proof#6.text: Across hosts a pool grows only by adding: each host's members are joined, and a host that removes one changes only its own copy.

beat:protocol/simple/proof#7.text: A cache is worked out from signed inputs, so it can be thrown away and rebuilt, and without it the hive gives the same answer, only slower.
